opus-5.5.text:
Well, first of all, thank you for having me.

You see, much of what people currently get excited about, the large language models and so on, is AI that sits behind a screen. It processes text, it writes emails, it summarizes documents, it helps with programming. That is very useful, but it touches only a small part of what matters. Most of the world economy is not about manipulating symbols on a screen. It is about manipulating matter: building houses, growing food, making machines, repairing pipes, caring for elderly people. A large share of global GDP is in this physical world, and so far AI has barely touched it.

Physical AI is also much harder. A language model can learn from the entire internet, a gigantic pile of text that humans have produced over decades. But there is no comparable internet for a robot that must learn to tie shoelaces or to fold laundry or to assemble a smartphone. The robot must interact with the world, make mistakes, and learn from the consequences of its own actions. This is the real reinforcement learning problem, and it is the problem my team and I have been interested in since around 1990, when we first built recurrent neural networks that learned a predictive world model, and a controller that used this model to plan. Today people call such things "world models," and they are becoming very fashionable again.

What's more, such a system should not only learn what it is told. It should be curious. It should invent its own experiments to figure out how the world works, just like a baby who plays with toys and learns physics that way. Back in 1990 we had artificial curiosity: one network generates actions, the other predicts the consequences, and the first is rewarded for discovering things the second cannot yet predict. That's how you get an agent that goes out and actively learns about the physical world, rather than passively absorbing data.

And then, looking further ahead, physical AI is what eventually allows AI to build more of itself. Imagine a little factory that can produce copies of itself, including the robots that run the factory. Once you have that, it scales like nothing before. And of course most of the physical resources are not here on our small planet, but out there in space, where there's far more matter and energy. Robots don't need oxygen; they'll be much better suited to that environment than humans are. So in the long run, I believe physical AI is the step that takes intelligence beyond the screen, beyond the Earth, and out into the universe.

So that's why I think it's so important: it's where most of the economic value is, it's where the hardest unsolved learning problems are, and it's where the long-term future of intelligence lies.

r001.rationale: The response describes a factory producing copies of itself and its robots, but does not identify learning to operate existing machinery as the route to replication.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize a machine that can operate all human-operated machines as a new kind of life.

r003.rationale: It does not argue that operating existing machinery requires only limited intelligence rather than superintelligence.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose using virtual AI's machine-learning methods to help societies of robots improve themselves.

r005.rationale: It mentions abundant matter and energy in space and separately describes self-replicating factories, but does not clearly connect extraterrestrial raw materials to those systems' expansion beyond Earth.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the real world is where intelligence came from, and it is where the hard problems remain. Everything we have done so far with large language models is, in a sense, easy. You take the text that humans have already written, you compress it, you predict the next word. That is passive learning from a fixed corpus. It is impressive, but it is not what a child does, and it is not what evolution produced.

A child does not learn by reading the internet. A child has a body, and it conducts experiments. It pushes a cup off the table to see what happens. It learns that its own actions have consequences in a physical world that pushes back. This is active learning, and the data is not given to you. You have to go and generate it yourself through your own behavior. That is the setting of reinforcement learning, which we have worked on since the early nineties, and it is a much harder problem, because the world is only partially observable, the feedback is sparse, and mistakes can be costly.

Now, why do I consider this so important? Several reasons. First, almost all of the economy is physical. Manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, construction, care for the elderly. Chatbots touch only a thin layer on top of this. The machine that can learn to repair a pipe or assemble a device it has never seen before, that is where the real transformation happens. Second, physical AI forces us to solve the fundamental scientific questions. An agent in the real world must build a model of that world, a world model, and use it to plan. It must be curious. In 1990 we already had artificial curiosity, where a controller is rewarded for discovering things that surprise its own predictive model, so the agent invents its own experiments like a little scientist. In the text domain you can get away without this. In the physical domain you cannot.

And third, I have a longer view. I have said for many decades that AI will not stay confined to this planet. The physical universe is enormous, and most of its resources are not here. An intelligence that can act in the physical world, that can build, replicate, and explore, is one that can eventually expand beyond Earth, where the real estate and energy are nearly unlimited. Language models will not do that. Robots that learn will.

So for me, physical AI is not one application among many. It is the return to the original problem that we always wanted to solve, a general-purpose learning machine that acts in the real world and improves itself through experience.

r001.rationale: The response says physical AI could repair or assemble things and that robots could build and replicate, but it does not identify learning to operate civilization’s existing machinery as the route.

r002.rationale: It describes a general-purpose learning machine that acts in the real world, but does not characterize a machine operating all machinery humans use as a new kind of life.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the intelligence needed for robotic self-replication with superintelligence or argue that learning to operate existing machinery would suffice.

r004.rationale: It mentions reinforcement learning, curiosity, and robots improving through experience, but does not propose applying virtual AI methods to societies of robots so they can improve themselves.

r005.rationale: It says most of the physical universe’s resources are beyond Earth and mentions expansion, building, and replication, but does not identify extraterrestrial raw materials as the basis for self-replicating robotic systems.

astra-6.text:
Because intelligence is not just about recognizing patterns or producing text. It is also about acting, observing the consequences, and learning how to achieve goals. In the physical world, your actions change what you will observe next. You have to learn this interaction.

Think of a robot learning to manipulate an unfamiliar object. It needs some understanding of what will happen if it pushes or lifts it. It can learn a predictive model of its world, use that model to plan, and improve the model when reality surprises it. That brings together perception, prediction, and control.

And the practical opportunities are enormous: machines that help manufacture things, perform difficult or dangerous work, and assist people in their daily lives. Much of what we want to accomplish requires changing the physical world. An intelligent system that can do that reliably can be tremendously useful.

r002.rationale: It does not describe a machine capable of operating all machines humans operate or characterize such a machine as a new kind of life.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss robotic self-replication or compare the required intelligence with superintelligence.

r004.rationale: It mentions learning and predictive models, but does not propose applying virtual-AI machine-learning methods to societies of robots improving themselves.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention extraterrestrial raw materials or expansion beyond Earth.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the real world is where intelligence ultimately has to prove useful. A system that produces text can help us think about a problem, but a robot can act: manipulate objects, conduct experiments, build things, or assist somebody in daily life.

And acting introduces a very important feedback loop. The system does something, observes the consequences, and learns to predict what will happen next. It can use this predictive model to plan actions that achieve its goals. But it can also choose actions that reveal something new—experiments that improve its understanding of the world.

Think of a baby. It does not learn only by listening to descriptions. It moves, touches things, and discovers what it can control. For artificial intelligence, this connection between learning and acting is enormously powerful. It is also how we can turn improvements in software into improvements in the physical conditions of our lives.

r001.rationale: The response says robots can manipulate objects, conduct experiments, build things, and learn from acting, but it does not identify learning to operate civilization’s existing machinery as a route to self-replicating machine systems.

r002.rationale: It describes robots as able to act in the physical world, but does not characterize a machine able to operate all machinery humans operate as a new kind of life.

r004.rationale: It mentions predictive models and learning through action, but does not propose using virtual-AI machine-learning methods to help robot societies improve themselves.
